segments.text: Right now, you can find thousands of tech experts making incredibly confident, hyper-specific
predictions about exactly where artificial intelligence is heading.
You generally have two camps.
You have the AI optimists, who envision an automated utopia, and the AI warriors, who
are preparing for a digital apocalypse.
But if you look at the historical track record of extreme certainty, the actual outcomes that
shape society are rarely the ones the experts see coming.
To understand why those rigid forecasts usually fall apart, we need to look backward, far
away from modern servers and code.
The best way to see it is a true story about rats.
In 1902, the city of Hanoi was rapidly modernizing.
The colonial government laid down miles of new state-of-the-art sewer pipes.
Unfortunately, those dark, protected tunnels provided the perfect breeding ground for
a massive rat infestation.
City officials devised what looked like a mathematically flawless solution.
They created a bounty system, offering citizens a small cash payment for every severed rat
tail handed in.
Initially, the metrics looked phenomenal.
Tales poured into government offices by the thousands on a daily basis.
But shortly after the program launched, citizens started noticing healthy, completely tailless
rats screwing around the city streets.
The math had a biological loophole.
A rat can survive perfectly fine without its tail.
And more importantly, it can keep making more rat babies.
The rat hunters figured out that killing the animal destroyed their own supply chain.
So, they caught the rats, clipped the tails to collect the cash, and released them back
into the sewers to breed.
A dead rat pays once.
A live rat pays forever.
Some local entrepreneurs realized hunting wild rats was too much work, so they bypassed
the sewers entirely and set up dedicated rat breeding farms.
The government eventually caught onto the scam and completely scrapped the bounty program.
They were left with a literal mountain of severed tails in their offices, but the actual living
rat population in Hanoi was significantly higher than before the bounty started.
But the real goal was fewer rats, and the program encouraged people to keep rats alive.
Hanoi's plan was fewer rats.
The unexpected result was more rats.
If we look at this graphic detailing historical plans, we can see this pattern repeats.
Here are two more unexpected results.
One welcome surprise, and one costly mistake.
Take SMS or text messaging.
Engineers originally built it for the narrow, utilitarian purpose of sending short diagnostic
messages over early mobile networks.
Its creators had absolutely no expectation it would gain traction with the public, but
young people got hold of it and turned texting into a daily global communication habit.
Or consider biology.
Australia deliberately imported cane toads with a highly specific agricultural job to eat
the beetles that were destroying their sugar cane crops.
The toads barely controlled the beetles at all.
Instead, they fed on native wildlife, poisoned the predators that tried to eat them, and reproduced
until they spread completely across the country.
Whether you are writing code or managing an ecosystem, the exact function you design is
frequently overrun by how users and environments adapt to it.
Now point that historical track record directly at the AI experts making today's headlines.
The predictions we hear from optimists and warriors alike are smart, heavily researched,
and informed, but they are likely aiming at the wrong target.
The most significant impact AI will have on your life over the next few decades, good
or bad, is probably something no researcher in any lab or academic camp has even thought
of yet.
That baseline unpredictability is not a reason to fear the future.
It is a reason to walk into it with your eyes open, fully recognizing that uncertainty
is part of the process.
You don't need a perfect forecast.
You need to watch how real people actually start using these tools, and focus on building
durable skills that hold their value even when the forecast changes.
As this final text banner highlights, some of the biggest results are the ones nobody
predicted.
That's the best reason to stay curious.
